November
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 3
A club runs solely on the efforts of volunteers.
Volunteers are not just needed for board positions, but for all of the activities of the club from
setting up chairs at a meeting, hauling out and
connecting “the gear”, running the video equipment, providing content for the newsletter and
website, getting accredited so that you can do a
turning demo for the club, or making a presentation. The great news is that we have another very
strong signup of keen members for this term. For
those of you that are newer to the Guild please
don’t be bashful about stepping forward. Your
participation is needed.
At our last Guild night Cathy Friesen presented an
inspiring exploration of how she is making an urn
for her Mom’s ashes. Cathy has put considerable
thought into the technical challenges of crafting a
vessel which will have a special scene that was
dear to her mom, depicted on the interior of the
vessel. Once sealed, it will be a special memento
just for her mom! This is the first time I’ve heard
of someone hiding their work from view – very
intriguing. It was a very personal and touching
presentation with lots of insight into the challenges of designing and making of the piece. Thank
you Cathy!
“My work is not good enough.” “I need to improve before I bring something to show.” These
are sometimes thoughts from newer turners. We
all start out at the same point, somewhat clueless
and without developed skills. We can all relate –
we’ve all been there. For novices and old-hands,
learning and understanding go both ways. We
feed off of each other. Also, your colleagues really
do want to see what you are making and see what
interests you! Oh, and one more thing, bringing in
show and tell or President’s Challenge items gets
you into the prize draw!!! Please remember, this
is not a competition.
January’s President’s Challenge is less weird than
usual: “A lidded container”. I’m also putting out
February’s challenge as it might be a little more
challenging and builds on the January challenge. It
shall be “A Tea Pot”. What constitutes a teapot? A
teapot has a container, a lid, a spout, and a handle. Feel free to incorporate multi-media into
your project. I am also advised that in the world
of collectable teapots that they do not necessarily
need to actually function, so don’t stress out
about that. The key is to make it appear as a teapot. Your friendly Internet search engines have
plenty of ideas as do the major museum and art
gallery sites – they are all searchable.
For now, may your shop floor be smothered in
fresh shavings,
Steve

November
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 4
Because we are not having a monthly meeting in
December, this will be the last newsletter of 2022.
This month’s newsletter is a bit shorter than normal, but certainly not short on some stellar content.
To complement her awesome presentation at our
October monthly meeting, Cathy Friesen has submitted an equally awesome and detailed article
recounting her very personal creative process in
the creation of a cremation urn for her parents.
Sheila returns with an article about AAW’s Women
in Turning (WIT) program, the benefits that WIT
offer, and her involvement with WIT as a new
turner.
Tony Tavenor has submitted a heartfelt article
about his experience taking up woodturning in
Newfoundland during the pandemic and how he
became involved with the GVWG. I’m sure many of
you will be nodding as you read his story, remembering your own journeys as a newly obsessed
woodturner.
I’m hoping that more of you, regardless of our skill
level, will be inspired to write an article whether it
be an account of your own experiences learning a
new skill, documenting the creation one of your
projects, a book or tool review or whatever you
have on your mind that is relevant to our art and
craft.
The October Tech Talk meeting would have taken
place on Halloween evening. That seemed like a
scary prospect so the meeting was postponed until
this month. Therefor, there is no regular Tech Talk
article this month.
Steve
Triangle Box
White Oak, 4” x 3.5”
I made my first triangle box to meet a 2021 President's Challenge (Re-purposed). I enjoyed working
out how to make the box and then presenting it at
one of our pandemic ZOOM sessions. It is textured
using both sand-blasting and wire brushing and
then "dry-brushed" using a technique I learn in Art
Liestman's Texturing and Coloring" workshop. Finally, the top is a piece of bamboo from my wife's
beautiful garden.

When my parents both passed away in 2007/2008 I
started searching the internet for nice urns that
would hold their ashes. The ones I liked best were
all made of wood. After 10 years of turning I finally
felt that I was experienced enough to turn them
urns that I would be happy with.
The Design
Scanning the internet I found a design that could
be turned as 2 bowls, giving me easy access to the
inside so that I could incorporate a rainbow, the
tree of life and the image of light shining down
from above through the clouds.
Cremation Urn Sizing
The following website guides you through sizing. It
converts the weight of the person to volume of water which I changed to cups of rice. Measure the
rice into a Ziploc bag which will give you a good
visual representation of how big your vessel will
need to be.
https://www.mainelyurns.com/what-sizecremation-urn.html
Enter the weight of your loved one and then "Calculate."
Here is what I learned…
Urns need to be sized to accept given amounts
of cremains based upon the formula of 1 cubic
inch per pound of live weight at the time of
death. Cremains must be sealed to prevent
water vapor from infusing the mass because
otherwise the powder will become like a rock.
The mortuary will put the ashes in a dense
plastic bag that gets heat-sealed, so your urn's
volume needs to be increased to accept the
bag and the opening will need to be large
enough to allow insertion.
Prepping The Wood
I used the crotch of a
Japanese Cherry Tree
which I dried outside,
standing upright, undercover for over a
year.
A Center Finder is just
a simple piece of plastic with circles on it.
But it is very useful for
finding the center of
your blank on a regular or irregular piece of wood. When using a faceplate this is very important as you can’t adjust it
once you have screwed it
to the faceplate.
After rough turning the 2
bowls I painted both
pieces completely with
end sealer, packed them
into a cardboard box surrounded by the wet shavings that had been generated by the rough turning, closed the box and
stored it outside, under cover for several weeks.
Every 2 weeks I opened the box, inspected the
pieces for mold growth and fluffed the shavings.

Carving the Top
I used photos of hydrangeas and work of Dixie
Biggs to draw the petals onto the top tenon.
This is the set-up for this process
•
I set up a work table on the lathe where the
lighting is good.
•
Table from an old IKEA shelf pressed between
the headstock and the banjo
•
Working out in the shop means there are no
dust issues.
•
I use an old bathtub floor mat to keep the work
from slipping.
•
The dust falls through the holes which means a
clean working area.
•
I have my reference pictures handy for quick
review.
•
Sit on a bar stool
Then I burned the outline and began carving the
petals giving them a 3-D effect.
If you want to see some real artistry in wood carving I encourage you to visit the Richmond Carvers
website and view the galleries. Their work is awe
inspiring.
https://www.richmondcarvers.com/
Securing the top in the Cole Jaws with plastic wrap
I burned in a defining line between the flowers and
the vessel. This was to prevent the finishing mediums from running into each other.
Using acrylic paints and India ink pens I painted the
Hydrangeas.

So what is the AAW’s Women in turning program
anyways? And why might you be interested?
The Women In Turning (WIT) is a committee within
the AAW (American Association of Woodturners)
and as stated on their webpage, “bringing together
women worldwide who share a passion for
woodturning. WIT is dedicated to encouraging and
assisting women in their pursuit of turning, to sharing ideas and processes to further members’ skills
and creativity, and to increasing the participation
of women in the field of woodturning.”
After being encouraged by so many amazing turners I met during the Worldwide Woodturners Symposium in August 2020, I joined the AAW. This was
just before becoming a member of our local chapter, GVWG. When I finally became a member of
the Greater Vancouver Woodturners Guild, I was a
member but a moment before being encouraged
to take on the WIT Liaison role, and I am so glad
that I did. It has been about 2 years now of turning, learning, and discovering my own creative
journey. February 2023, at the Guild’s next AGM,
after two years of officially being in the role, it is a
perfect opportunity to pass the torch so that another can learn, discovery and add to their own
journey. Might you take on this encouraging role?
Energy in converts to opportunities for creative energy out.
Do you know there are several ways in which the
WIT AAW encourages woodturners? One is
through their grant programs, which is constantly
evolving.
https://www.woodturner.org/Woodturner/WIT/
WIT-Home-Page.aspx?
100134f70e4f=4#100134f70e4f
There is a AAW Membership Grant to encourage
women to join the AAW with limited number of
WIT sponsored AAW memberships for a one-year
AAW General Membership. To be eligible, a grant
recipient must be a woman who has never previously been a member of the AAW. Grants are currently limited to no more than two women, per
chapter, per quarter. In the past, on behalf of new
members, I have made grant applications. If you
are new to GVWG and not been a member of the
AAW and this is something that may interest you,
please reach out to me at wit@gvwg.ca and we can
begin the application process. This gives membership access to an amazing assortment of resources
and information which can be especially helpful for
turners who what to pursue and explore even
more.
But that is not all. There are also “Calls” for Professional Outreach Programs, Special Interest Sessions
for the AAW Symposiums, AAW Online Demonstrators and Presenters, and POP Artist Showcases…
while some deadlines for 2023 have past, others
are ongoing and there is always 2024.
Signing onto the WIT website to prepare this article, I also learned of a new “Pay It Forward” campaign to encourage and retain women in
woodturning with the introduction of 60-day guest
memberships and ideas of how one might go about
adding even more turners to the mix.
This is in addition to the fabulous events and archives hosted by the WIT Committee that are available to ALL AAW members. Recently, listening to
Helga Winter present on November 5th I was encouraged by the wide variety of creative directions
she has pursued over the years. Betty Scarpino,
another amazingly talented creative, has written an
article about Helga too, The Vocabulary of Experience.
https://www.woodturner.org/Woodturner/WIT/
WIT-Home-Page.aspx?
100134f70e4f=7#100134f70e4f
Additionally, my personal involvement with the
WIT committee has included promoting and participating in two of the WIT Exchanges, with the 2022
one giving me the opportunity to partner with
Shawn and Pippa, two members within the GVWG,
and turning together in person. I have also tapped
into and watched a bunch of WIT events, both in
(Continued on page 15)

November
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 15
person or from the archives and was struck how
many of the personal stories resonated for me too.
Most of all, I appreciate the community of
woodturners for being example of how to lift and
support turners on their journey. While there are
some common themes and places people can go
with their turning, there is as many varieties and
opportunities as there are creative people who just
love to explore and make.
(Continued from page 14)
Two things happened. Covid hit and I turned 60.
What to do. I began thinking about how to mark
the birthday in the era of isolation. Newfoundland
had some of the most stringent quarantine rules in
the country at the time.
I looked up on a shelf in my kitchen and admired
the 3 turned vases gifted to me by a friend's father
and it hit me. Grade 9, my only year of industrial
arts. In the corner of the room was a lathe and it
intrigued me. I couldn't wait to give it a try.
Unfortunately, our teacher was involved in an accident and the fill-in instructor had a background in
teaching religious studies. After he injured himself
twice with the shop equipment all hopes of turning
evaporated.
Now was the time to give it a go. Life was handing
me the perfect opportunity. I was going to turn
wood! Finally,
To start I called a friend who had been turning
since his teens. I invited myself to his shop to see if
I would even like the work. We spent 5 hours in an
unheated garage in February and I made a small
platter and a pen, with the closest of hands on supervision. It was as much fun as I imagined.
Next step, get a lathe. I did a little reading, watched
some videos, got confused, and ordered a lathe.
The next day I walked into my medium sized shed
with a skidoo, table saw, 2 snow blowers, no heat,
1 plug in, 1 light, and 1 small window. This wasn't
going to work. It took me 10 minutes of moving
things to use my table saw! A work space was
needed.
My wife and I discussed a little 10X10 shed. It didn't fit in with her idea of a nice looking addition.
She modified my plans a bit ( another story there)
To start the project I cleared a 1/4 acre area of forested land on my property and saved the wood for
future turning (yes, the idea grew well beyond a
10X10 shed), hired 3 guys, a tractor, and frantically
sought the best pandemic adjusted lumber prices.
Three months later the old shed was gone and the
new Shed Plus was ready to go.
I ordered gouges, a chuck with a series of jaws, and
purchased a bench grinder. I was proud I had
thought of the need to sharpen. Everything arrived
and I set it all up. I watched more YouTube videos.
It was time.
I bravely entered the shop, put on my face shield,
mounted a piece of cherry, and began my
woodturning career. The face shield is important, I
decided, as the piece flew past my head. Back to
YouTube I go.
About this time I was speaking to my cousin Brian
who, coincidently, started to woodturn.
He told me about the Greater Vancouver
Woodturners Guild and the virtual Zoom meetings.
Sounded great and he arranged an invite to the
next meeting.
It was 11:30 pm with the time difference and I sat
there with notebook in hand. The real world of
woodturning opened up to me.I saw a group of
people with an unbelievable cache of knowledge
willing to let it flow. I learned things immediately.
Things like I had just cut a 1/4 acre of forest completely wrong for the best preservation as blanks. I
learned that there were low speed grinders and
CBN wheels and HSS steel to prevent the extremely
(Continued on page 16)

November
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 16
fast melting that occurred with the first gouge I
"sharpened".
With each meeting new pearls were gleaned. I
learned not to trust the YouTube experts, although
I kind of already knew that after the first flying
piece of wood when I reviewed the video I just
watched and decided I had done everything just
like the "expert" demonstrated.
I also learned a lot of non-woodturning things. Like,
people in Vancouver voluntarily go sailing in December. Those Dessert Talks can lead you anywhere.
The demonstrations from far and away were not
only exciting, but made me see woodturning as a
community. This was echoed in the obvious closeness of the Guild members on the Zoom calls.
Successes started to happen. I took a hands-on
course for 4 days in Nova Scotia. I bought some
books. I practiced and made a lot of wood shavings. It was paying off. I made coasters to protect
the floor from the legs of a metal bench, hole
punches for cans, snowmen, Christmas trees, candle holders and an Easter Egg in a cup.It wasn't expert quality work but it was good enough that I
was enjoying the process and could see improvement.
Then came my proudest projects. I made a spin
top, a pull toy, and a race car for my new grandson.
And he plays with them!
The only downside was the late nights. In my former life I was used to long hours, often working 48
hours without sleeping. But I have been retired
from that for 6 years and I have aged and am not
suited for concentrating late at night anymore. I
had to find alternatives.
And that is when I found out how truly Incredible
the Greater Vancouver Woodturners Guild really is.
I thought, if there is one there must be others closer to my time zone. I searched the AAW website
for chapters across this country. There were many
listed and some in much more convenient time
zones. I reached out to several from the contact
information on the website. Not a single response.
They were all radio silent. Had they folded or was
the contact information obsolete? I talked to a few
people who were past members of some of these
guilds and they were not aware of any activity in
the groups from even before the pandemic. Sad.
It was at this time I realized I had stumbled upon a
unique situation. I had found a group of superb
woodturners. They were very welcoming to newcomers. They were excited to share knowledge and
had real joy in seeing others successes. How unselfish and heartwarming.
Add to this you are a tight knit social group so your
personal friendships kept you going. The common
link is woodturning, but the cross section of expertise is an unbelievable resource. Bizarre esoteric questions can be answered immediately and
with authority.
The third component is the interest and enthusiasm that allowed you to overcome and thrive in
the Pandemic Era. Your quick and effective shift to
online format may seem obvious to you, but most
groups did not grasp the option. You are able to
pivot and are trying mixed live/remote meetings so
you can keep the best of both worlds.
It saddens me that I won't be able to continue with
the group. I will keep turning. I have not found a
local group but I have a plan. I will be joining the
AAW and will be setting aside time each week to
review the educational material there and dedicate
practice time to the lessons given. I am going to
reach out to the local turners for advice and maybe
we can start getting together. Who knows, maybe
we will be our own guild one day.
I just wanted to say thanks for the education, support, and warm feelings. I hope you all appreciate
what a unique thing you have with the Greater
Vancouver Woodturners Guild. If you are ever on
the West coast of Newfoundland Drop by. Maybe
we can make some shavings together.
(Continued from page 15)

 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock

with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
For more information on woodturning
safety please visit the AAW’s Woodturning Safety webpage.
